notes: 15 independently written six-mark AQA-style challenge problems, not verbatim AQA paper text.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Extended independent practice
markPoints: Weight mg=49.05 N and its downslope component is mg sin25°≈20.73 N.
Normal reaction R=mg cos25°≈44.45 N.
Friction μR≈8.89 N, directed down the slope.
Net uphill force=60−20.73−8.89≈30.38 N.
Acceleration a=F/m≈6.08 m s⁻².
From rest s=½at²≈27.35 m after 3.0 s.
questions.modelAnswer: Weight mg=49.05 N and its downslope component is mg sin25°≈20.73 N. Normal reaction R=mg cos25°≈44.45 N. Friction μR≈8.89 N, directed down the slope. Net uphill force=60−20.73−8.89≈30.38 N. Acceleration a=F/m≈6.08 m s⁻². From rest s=½at²≈27.35 m after 3.0 s.
questions.prompt: A 5.0 kg crate is pulled up a rough slope inclined at 25° to the horizontal by a 60 N force parallel to the slope. The coefficient of friction is 0.20. Calculate its normal reaction, friction, net force and acceleration. Starting from rest, how far does it travel in 3.0 s? Use g=9.81 m s⁻².

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Extended independent practice
markPoints: Ideal gas equation is pV=nRT and the initial volume is 0.02493 m³.
At 450 K the final volume is 0.03740 m³.
Work at constant pressure is W=pΔV≈1.25×10³ J.
For a monatomic ideal gas ΔU=3nRΔT/2≈1.87×10³ J.
By the first law Q=ΔU+W.
Heat supplied Q≈3.12×10³ J.
questions.modelAnswer: Ideal gas equation is pV=nRT and the initial volume is 0.02493 m³. At 450 K the final volume is 0.03740 m³. Work at constant pressure is W=pΔV≈1.25×10³ J. For a monatomic ideal gas ΔU=3nRΔT/2≈1.87×10³ J. By the first law Q=ΔU+W. Heat supplied Q≈3.12×10³ J.
questions.prompt: One mole of an ideal monatomic gas initially at 300 K and 1.00×10⁵ Pa is heated to 450 K at constant pressure. Take R=8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Calculate initial and final volumes, work done by the gas, its internal energy change and the heat energy transferred to it.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Extended independent practice
markPoints: Cross-sectional area A=π(0.00015)²=7.07×10⁻⁸ m².
Resistivity ρ=gradient×A≈9.90×10⁻⁸ Ω m.
Intercept from 0.80−1.40×0.50=0.10 Ω.
Expected resistance at 2.00 m is 1.40×2.00+0.10=2.90 Ω.
The non-zero intercept indicates contact/lead resistance and should not be included in the sample's resistivity.
questions.modelAnswer: Gradient (2.20−0.80)/(1.50−0.50)=1.40 Ω m⁻¹. Cross-sectional area A=π(0.00015)²=7.07×10⁻⁸ m². Resistivity ρ=gradient×A≈9.90×10⁻⁸ Ω m. Intercept from 0.80−1.40×0.50=0.10 Ω. Expected resistance at 2.00 m is 1.40×2.00+0.10=2.90 Ω. The non-zero intercept indicates contact/lead resistance and should not be included in the sample's resistivity.
questions.prompt: A metal wire gives 0.80 Ω at length 0.50 m and 2.20 Ω at length 1.50 m. Its diameter is 0.30 mm. Assuming a constant contact resistance, calculate the gradient of a resistance-length graph, resistivity and the contact resistance. Predict the measured resistance at 2.00 m and explain why the intercept matters.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Extended independent practice
markPoints: Area is 30 cm²=3.0×10⁻³ m².
Flux change per turn is AΔB=0.003×0.50=1.50×10⁻³ Wb.
Change in flux linkage NΔΦ=200×0.0015=0.300 Wb turns.
Induced emf magnitude is 0.300/0.050=6.00 V.
By Lenz's law the induced current would oppose the increase in magnetic flux.
Doubling the change time halves the emf magnitude to 3.00 V.
questions.modelAnswer: Area is 30 cm²=3.0×10⁻³ m². Flux change per turn is AΔB=0.003×0.50=1.50×10⁻³ Wb. Change in flux linkage NΔΦ=200×0.0015=0.300 Wb turns. Induced emf magnitude is 0.300/0.050=6.00 V. By Lenz's law the induced current would oppose the increase in magnetic flux. Doubling the change time halves the emf magnitude to 3.00 V.
questions.prompt: A coil has 200 turns, each with area 30 cm², and its axis is parallel to a uniform field. The field changes from 0.15 T to 0.65 T in 0.050 s. Calculate the magnitude of induced emf and explain its direction. Predict the emf if the same flux change takes twice as long.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Extended independent practice
markPoints: Initial HCl moles are 0.0500×0.400=0.0200 mol.
Remaining HCl moles are 0.0200×0.250=0.00500 mol.
HCl consumed by carbonate is 0.0150 mol.
Using CaCO3+2HCl→CaCl2+CO2+H2O, carbonate moles are 0.00750 mol.
questions.modelAnswer: Initial HCl moles are 0.0500×0.400=0.0200 mol. Remaining HCl moles are 0.0200×0.250=0.00500 mol. HCl consumed by carbonate is 0.0150 mol. Using CaCO3+2HCl→CaCl2+CO2+H2O, carbonate moles are 0.00750 mol. Carbonate mass=0.00750×100.1=0.75075 g. Percentage purity=(0.75075/0.800)×100=93.8%.
questions.prompt: An 0.800 g sample containing calcium carbonate and inert impurities is treated with 50.0 cm³ of 0.400 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid. Excess HCl requires 20.0 cm³ of 0.250 mol dm⁻³ NaOH to neutralise. Find the mass and percentage purity of CaCO3 in the sample. Use Mr(CaCO3)=100.1.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Extended independent practice
markPoints: Atomise Mg: +148 kJ mol⁻¹.
One oxygen atom requires half of O2 dissociation: +249 kJ mol⁻¹.
Ionise Mg twice: +738+1451=+2189 kJ mol⁻¹.
Add oxygen electron affinities: −141+744=+603 kJ mol⁻¹.
Born–Haber sum is −602=(148+249+2189+603)+ΔHlatt.
Lattice enthalpy of formation is −3791 kJ mol⁻¹; half O2 forms one O atom per MgO.
questions.modelAnswer: Atomise Mg: +148 kJ mol⁻¹. One oxygen atom requires half of O2 dissociation: +249 kJ mol⁻¹. Ionise Mg twice: +738+1451=+2189 kJ mol⁻¹. Add oxygen electron affinities: −141+744=+603 kJ mol⁻¹. Born–Haber sum is −602=(148+249+2189+603)+ΔHlatt. Lattice enthalpy of formation is −3791 kJ mol⁻¹; half O2 forms one O atom per MgO.
questions.prompt: For forming MgO(s), ΔHf=−602 kJ mol⁻¹. Use the data (kJ mol⁻¹): Mg atomisation +148; O2 bond enthalpy +498; Mg ionisations +738 and +1451; O first electron affinity −141, second +744. Calculate the lattice enthalpy of formation and explain why O2 bond enthalpy is halved.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Extended independent practice
markPoints: Doubling [A] alone doubles rate, so first order in A.
Doubling [B] quadruples rate, so second order in B.
Rate law is rate=k[A][B]², third order overall.
Units of k are dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹.
questions.modelAnswer: Doubling [A] alone doubles rate, so first order in A. Doubling [B] quadruples rate, so second order in B. Rate law is rate=k[A][B]², third order overall. From experiment 1, k=(2.0×10⁻⁴)/(0.10×0.10²)=0.20. Units of k are dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹. At [A]=0.30 and [B]=0.20, rate=0.20×0.30×0.20²=2.4×10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
questions.prompt: For A+B→products, measured initial rates (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹) are: experiment 1 [A]=0.10, [B]=0.10, rate=2.0×10⁻⁴; experiment 2 [A]=0.20, [B]=0.10, rate=4.0×10⁻⁴; experiment 3 [A]=0.10, [B]=0.20, rate=8.0×10⁻⁴. Determine both orders, the rate equation, k with units and the predicted rate at [A]=0.30 and [B]=0.20.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Extended independent practice
markPoints: Convert ΔS=0.220 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Use ΔG=ΔH−TΔS.
At ΔG=0, threshold T=78/0.220≈355 K.
Negative ΔG predicts thermodynamic feasibility but not reaction speed, which depends on activation energy.
questions.modelAnswer: Convert ΔS=0.220 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Use ΔG=ΔH−TΔS. At 298 K, ΔG=78−298×0.220=+12.44 kJ mol⁻¹. At ΔG=0, threshold T=78/0.220≈355 K. At 400 K, ΔG=78−400×0.220=−10.0 kJ mol⁻¹. Negative ΔG predicts thermodynamic feasibility but not reaction speed, which depends on activation energy.
questions.prompt: A chemical process has ΔH=+78 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS=+220 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, taken as temperature independent. Calculate ΔG at 298 K, the approximate threshold temperature for thermodynamic feasibility, and ΔG at 400 K. Explain why a feasible reaction may still be slow.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Extended independent practice
markPoints: Box dimensions are x by (30−2x) by (30−2x), with 0<x<15.
Volume V=x(30−2x)².
Derivative dV/dx=(30−2x)(30−6x).
Stationary points satisfy x=5 or x=15, but x=15 is the boundary of a degenerate box.
Since V approaches zero at x→0 and x→15, and is positive inside, x=5 gives the maximum.
Maximum volume V=5×20²=2000 cm³.
questions.modelAnswer: Box dimensions are x by (30−2x) by (30−2x), with 0<x<15. Volume V=x(30−2x)². Derivative dV/dx=(30−2x)(30−6x). Stationary points satisfy x=5 or x=15, but x=15 is the boundary of a degenerate box. Since V approaches zero at x→0 and x→15, and is positive inside, x=5 gives the maximum. Maximum volume V=5×20²=2000 cm³.
questions.prompt: An open-topped box is made from a 30 cm by 30 cm sheet by removing squares of side x cm from each corner and folding up the sides. Prove that the maximum possible volume occurs when x=5 cm, and calculate that maximum volume. State the physical range of x.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Extended independent practice
markPoints: Under H0, X~Binomial(12,0.5); H0:p=0.5 and H1:p>0.5.
Because 10 heads were observed, calculate P(X≥10).
The one-tailed p-value is about 0.0193.
Since p-value<0.05, reject H0.
There is sufficient evidence at 5% that the probability of heads exceeds 0.5.
questions.modelAnswer: Under H0, X~Binomial(12,0.5); H0:p=0.5 and H1:p>0.5. Because 10 heads were observed, calculate P(X≥10). P(X≥10)=(66+12+1)/4096=79/4096. The one-tailed p-value is about 0.0193. Since p-value<0.05, reject H0. There is sufficient evidence at 5% that the probability of heads exceeds 0.5.
questions.prompt: A coin is suspected of being biased towards heads. In 12 independent tosses it produces 10 heads. At the 5% significance level carry out a one-tailed binomial test, giving hypotheses, p-value, decision and interpretation. You may use combinations C(12,10)=66, C(12,11)=12.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Extended independent practice
markPoints: P(fault)=0.02 and P(good)=0.98.
Bayes gives P(fault|flag)=0.0190/0.0974≈0.195.
Most components are good, so false positives can outnumber genuinely faulty flagged components.
questions.modelAnswer: P(fault)=0.02 and P(good)=0.98. P(flag and fault)=0.02×0.95=0.0190. P(flag and good)=0.98×0.08=0.0784. Total P(flag)=0.0190+0.0784=0.0974. Bayes gives P(fault|flag)=0.0190/0.0974≈0.195. Most components are good, so false positives can outnumber genuinely faulty flagged components.
questions.prompt: A screening system checks manufactured components. Two per cent are faulty. A faulty component is flagged with probability 0.95, whereas a good one is flagged with probability 0.08. Calculate the probability of a flag and the probability that a flagged component is faulty. Explain why the second probability is far below 95%.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Extended independent practice
markPoints: Equate x-coordinates: 1+2s=3, giving s=1.
Equate z-coordinates: s=1+t, giving t=0.
Both y-coordinates are then 1; intersection is (3,1,1).
Direction vectors are a=(2,−1,1) and b=(0,1,1).
Dot product a·b=0, so the lines meet at 90°.
Distance of the intersection from the origin is √(3²+1²+1²)=√11.

Direction vectors are a=(2,−1,1) and b=(0,1,1). Dot product a·b=0, so the lines meet at 90°. Distance of the intersection from the origin is √(3²+1²+1²)=√11.
questions.prompt: Two lines have vector equations r=(1,2,0)+s(2,−1,1) and r=(3,1,1)+t(0,1,1). Determine whether the lines intersect; if so find their meeting point, the angle between their direction vectors and the distance of the point from the origin.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Extended independent practice
questions.prompt: Lattice dissociation enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹) are: CaCl₂ 2223 (perfect ionic) / 2237 (Born–Haber); KCl 690 / 701; AgCl 770 / 905. In a coherent six-mark answer, explain the relative lattice strengths and what the differences between the perfect ionic model and Born–Haber results reveal about bonding in all three compounds.
markPoints: CaCl₂ has the largest ideal lattice dissociation enthalpy: Ca²⁺ has a greater positive charge than K⁺ and Ag⁺.
Higher charge and small interionic separation lead to stronger electrostatic attractions and more energy required to dissociate CaCl₂.
Ag⁺ is smaller than K⁺, so AgCl has a higher theoretical lattice enthalpy than KCl due to shorter ionic separation.
CaCl₂ and KCl have small perfect-model/Born–Haber discrepancies (14 and 11 kJ mol⁻¹), consistent with predominantly ionic bonding.
AgCl has a much larger discrepancy (135 kJ mol⁻¹), suggesting greater covalent character than predicted by the perfect ionic model.
Ag⁺ distorts the Cl⁻ electron cloud (polarisation), creating shared electron density and covalent character that adds lattice stabilisation.
questions.modelAnswer: CaCl₂ has the largest ideal lattice dissociation enthalpy: Ca²⁺ has a greater positive charge than K⁺ and Ag⁺. Higher charge and small interionic separation lead to stronger electrostatic attractions and more energy required to dissociate CaCl₂. Ag⁺ is smaller than K⁺, so AgCl has a higher theoretical lattice enthalpy than KCl due to shorter ionic separation. CaCl₂ and KCl have small perfect-model/Born–Haber discrepancies (14 and 11 kJ mol⁻¹), consistent with predominantly ionic bonding. AgCl has a much larger discrepancy (135 kJ mol⁻¹), suggesting greater covalent character than predicted by the perfect ionic model. Ag⁺ distorts the Cl⁻ electron cloud (polarisation), creating shared electron density and covalent character that adds lattice stabilisation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Extended independent practice
questions.prompt: Draw and fully label a Born–Haber cycle for the formation of MgO(s) from Mg(s) and ½O₂(g). Include every atomisation, Mg first and second ionisation, O first and second electron affinity, intermediate gaseous species, any free electrons, lattice formation, direct standard enthalpy of formation, and correct endothermic/exothermic arrow directions. You can draw on paper then check your steps against the mark points.
markPoints: Overall standard formation: Mg(s) + ½O₂(g) → MgO(s), with ΔHf arrow connecting start to final ionic solid.
Correct atomisations: Mg(s) → Mg(g) and ½O₂(g) → O(g), with gaseous atoms and positive (+) endothermic arrows.
First ionisation of Mg: Mg(g) → Mg⁺(g) + e⁻, followed by second ionisation Mg⁺(g) → Mg²⁺(g) + e⁻, both endothermic.
Correct charge and electron accounting at the fully ionised intermediate stage: Mg²⁺(g) + O(g) + 2e⁻.
First and second electron affinities: O(g) + e⁻ → O⁻(g) (exothermic) and O⁻(g) + e⁻ → O²⁻(g) (endothermic), ending with Mg²⁺(g) + O²⁻(g).
Lattice formation Mg²⁺(g) + O²⁻(g) → MgO(s), shown as an exothermic downward arrow. Positive enthalpy arrows point up, negative down.
questions.modelAnswer: Overall standard formation: Mg(s) + ½O₂(g) → MgO(s), with ΔHf arrow connecting start to final ionic solid. Correct atomisations: Mg(s) → Mg(g) and ½O₂(g) → O(g), with gaseous atoms and positive (+) endothermic arrows. First ionisation of Mg: Mg(g) → Mg⁺(g) + e⁻, followed by second ionisation Mg⁺(g) → Mg²⁺(g) + e⁻, both endothermic. Correct charge and electron accounting at the fully ionised intermediate stage: Mg²⁺(g) + O(g) + 2e⁻. First and second electron affinities: O(g) + e⁻ → O⁻(g) (exothermic) and O⁻(g) + e⁻ → O²⁻(g) (endothermic), ending with Mg²⁺(g) + O²⁻(g). Lattice formation Mg²⁺(g) + O²⁻(g) → MgO(s), shown as an exothermic downward arrow. Positive enthalpy arrows point up, negative down.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Extended independent practice
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'An endothermic reaction cannot be feasible because energy is absorbed. If ΔG is negative, the reaction must occur quickly. Increasing temperature always makes reactions more feasible.' Discuss each claim using ΔG=ΔH−TΔS, the signs of ΔH and ΔS, activation energy and the role of a catalyst. [6 marks]
markPoints: Thermodynamic feasibility depends on the Gibbs relation ΔG=ΔH−TΔS; negative ΔG favours the forward change.
An endothermic reaction with ΔH positive can be feasible if ΔS is positive and TΔS exceeds ΔH.
For such a process, raising temperature can make ΔG negative even though energy is absorbed.
Negative ΔG predicts feasibility, not reaction speed; a high activation energy can make the reaction very slow.
A catalyst lowers activation energy and increases rate but does not alter ΔG of the overall reaction.
When ΔS is positive, increasing temperature lowers ΔG; when ΔS is negative, increasing temperature raises ΔG, so heating does not always improve feasibility.
questions.modelAnswer: Thermodynamic feasibility depends on ΔG=ΔH−TΔS. Even when ΔH is positive (endothermic), a sufficiently large positive ΔS at high T makes TΔS exceed ΔH and ΔG negative. A negative ΔG signals a thermodynamically favourable direction but does not mean the reaction is fast: a high activation-energy barrier can make the rate very slow. A catalyst lowers activation energy and raises rate, but does not change ΔG. Increasing temperature makes ΔG more negative only if ΔS is positive; if ΔS is negative, increasing temperature makes ΔG more positive. Thus all three claims are incorrect.
